2002-12.label: 2002-12 - Oil supply collapsed after a major strike in Venezuela

Energy producers.specific_notes:
1 month
Oil prices jumped immediately after the supply disruption, and energy producers reacted fast, delivering strong short-term gains.

3 months
As oil prices stayed elevated, energy companies continued to benefit from higher revenues, reinforcing the initial gains.

6 months
The supply shock translated into sustained profitability, with energy firms steadily compounding gains over the following months.

12 months
Even one year later, energy producers remained significantly ahead, showing that the shock had lasting effects rather than a short-lived spike.

Oil users (transport & airlines).specific_notes:
1 month - Small gain despite higher oil
Fuel costs rise immediately, but companies haven’t adjusted yet.
Transport firms still benefit from pre-shock contracts and delayed pricing, so the portfolio stays slightly positive in the first month.

3 months - Shock starts to bite
Higher oil prices begin to hurt margins.
Airlines and shippers feel the cost pressure, wiping out most gains as fuel expenses slowly pass through.

6 months - Adaptation kicks in
Companies adjust prices and operations.
Ticket prices, shipping rates, and efficiency measures improve profitability, leading to a clear recovery.

12 months - Strong recovery
The sector fully adapts to the new oil price level.
Higher transport prices and normalized demand outweigh fuel costs, resulting in strong gains over the year.

Defensive staples.specific_notes:
1 month - Short-term resilience
Essential goods demand stays stable.
Even as oil prices jump, consumers keep buying food and household products, limiting the immediate impact.

3 months - Cost pressure shows up
Higher transport and input costs squeeze margins.
Companies are slower to raise prices, leading to a temporary dip in performance.

6 months - Gradual pass-through
Firms begin adjusting prices and supply chains.
Cost increases are partially passed on to consumers, allowing profits to recover.

12 months - Steady, defensive recovery
Stability beats sensitivity.
Staples don’t benefit from oil shocks, but their predictable demand delivers steady gains once costs are absorbed.

Mixed exposure (producers + users).specific_notes:
1 month - Immediate benefit from balance
Winners offset losers.
Higher oil prices help producers right away, while users are only mildly hurt, leading to a solid early gain.

3 months - Short-term stabilization
Opposite forces cancel out.
Producer gains slow as oil stabilizes, while users face higher costs, keeping returns positive but muted.

6 months - Broad recovery
Both sides start contributing.
Producers benefit from sustained oil prices, and users adapt through pricing and efficiency, pushing returns higher.

12 months - Strong, diversified outcome
Diversification pays off.
Exposure to both sides of the oil market delivers strong gains with less volatility than pure producer or user portfolios.

Broad diversified mix.specific_notes:
(Oil +17.9% in the shock month; portfolio entry one month before)
1 month - Shock absorbed
The oil jump is cushioned.
Energy gains help, but exposure to non-energy sectors limits both upside and downside, resulting in a modest gain.
(+8.8%)

3 months - Balanced adjustment
Different sectors react at different speeds.
Oil-linked stocks cool off while the rest of the portfolio stabilizes, keeping returns positive but contained.
(+6.1%)

6 months - Broad recovery
The economy catches up.
As higher energy prices feed through the system, most sectors adapt, lifting the diversified portfolio.
(+24.8%)

12 months - Steady, diversified growth
No single bet, but strong overall performance.
Exposure across energy and non-energy sectors delivers solid long-term gains with lower volatility.
(+42.6%)

2008-05.label: 2008-05 - Oil prices surged as global demand outpaced oil production

Energy producers.specific_notes:
(Oil +12.5% in the shock month; entry one month before)
1 month - Late-stage oil rally lifts stocks
Oil prices spike further, and energy producers ride the momentum.
Higher spot prices immediately boost revenue expectations, leading to strong short-term gains as the oil boom continues.
(+19.4%)

3 months - Momentum fades
Oil prices remain high, but warning signs appear.
Concerns about slowing global demand and rising costs start to weigh on energy stocks, flattening gains despite still-elevated oil prices.
(+0.3%)

6 months - Oil boom turns into bust
The shock reverses violently.
As the global financial crisis intensifies, oil prices collapse and energy demand falls sharply. Producer stocks suffer massive losses as revenues and investment plans break down.
(−42.2%)

12 months - Crisis dominates fundamentals
Oil is no longer the main driver.
Even though oil prices stabilize somewhat, the broader financial crisis overwhelms the sector. Credit stress, collapsing demand, and balance-sheet pressure keep energy producers deeply underwater one year later.
(−54.5%)

(Oil +12.5% in the shock month; entry one month before)

3 months - Temporary stabilization

It’s no longer just about oil.
As the financial crisis unfolds, demand for travel and shipping collapses. Even if oil starts falling later, revenues drop faster than costs, driving deep losses.
(−8.4%)

12 months - Demand shock dominates
Cheap oil can’t save collapsing demand.
By one year out, the global recession has crushed transport volumes. Lower fuel prices arrive too late, leaving the sector with severe cumulative losses.
(−30.5%)
